splash.tagline: What AI coding assistants are, what they can do, and how to use any of them responsibly.

what.title: What is a coding assistant?
what.text: A coding assistant is an AI that helps you write, read, fix, and explain code. You describe what you want in plain language and it responds with code, explanations, or actions. Some only suggest text as you type. Others can act: open files, edit them, run commands, and check their own work.

meaning.title: What using one really means
bullets: You become the reviewer. Your job shifts from typing every line to deciding what is right.
You stay accountable. The tool drafts, you ship.
The more it can do, the more it can do wrong. Autonomy and risk grow together.
Clear instructions give clear results. Vague requests give vague code.

competitors.title: The landscape
rows: Terminal pair programmer that commits every change to git
Agent for terminal, IDEs, desktop, and web
Terminal, IDE, desktop, and cloud coding agent
AI code editor with Tab, chat, and an agent mode
Suggestions and chat in your editor, plus agent tasks
Standalone AI IDE with an agent

why.title: What to look for in any of them
bullets: Control: can you choose when it asks before editing files or running commands?
Privacy: where does your code go, and is it used for training?
Fit: does it work in the editor or terminal you already use?
Cost: is pricing per seat, per use, or bring-your-own key, and what are the limits?
Approval: is it on your organization's approved list?
why.note: No tool is best for everyone. Pick for your work, your team, and your rules.

disclaimer.title: Professional use: check with IT first
disclaimer.text: If you are using an AI coding assistant for work, check with your IT or security team before you use it. Your organization may restrict which tools are allowed, what data and code can be shared with them, and how the output may be used. It is your responsibility to follow those rules. This guide is general information, not legal, security, or compliance advice.

needs.label: Every change is a git commit

content.heading: Step 0: is it approved?
content.text: Before you compare features, check with your IT or security team. If a tool is not approved for work, it does not matter how good it is.
content.warn: Using an unapproved tool on work code can break company policy. It is your responsibility to check first.

content.heading: Tick what matters to you
content.note: This ranks tools by how many of your needs match what the vendors' docs describe. It is a starting point, not a verdict. Try your top two on a small real task.

content.heading: Score your own shortlist
content.text: Give each finalist 1 to 5 on every row, then add them up. Weigh the rows that matter most to you.
table: Is it allowed by IT? A no here ends the comparison.
Where does my code go? Is it used for training? Can I keep secrets out?
Can I make it ask before editing files or running commands?
Does it work in my editor or terminal, on my operating system?
Did it do well on a small real task from my own project?
Per seat, per use, or bring-your-own key? What are the limits?
Can I give it my team's rules and recipes?
Is there an admin, billing, and a plan for teams?

content.heading: At a glance
table: Terminal, VS Code, JetBrains, desktop, web
Big multi-file tasks and customizable workflows
Help while you code, plus agent tasks on GitHub
Set by GitHub and your plan
People who want AI built into the editor
Set by the product and your plan
Delegating tasks, including in the cloud
Free-tier terminal work and very large context
Git-friendly pairing with the model you choose
content.note: Details come from each vendor's own docs, read on 2 Oct 2026. This space moves fast, so check the vendor site before you decide.

content.heading: Which one should you pick?
bullets: Want help while you type in an editor: GitHub Copilot or Cursor.
Want to hand off a whole task and review the result: Claude Code, Codex, or an IDE agent like Cursor or Windsurf.
Want to pay little or nothing: Gemini CLI's free tier, GitHub Copilot Free, or Aider with a cheap model.
Want to choose or switch models freely: Aider or Cursor.
Work in a locked-down company: ask IT which tools are approved before you install anything.

content.heading: The same rules apply to all of them
bullets: Work on a git branch and commit before you start.
Read every change before you accept it.
Never paste secrets or customer data into any assistant.
Start with the most cautious permission setting, and check what the default is first.
content.warn: Every tool on these pages can be wrong, and the ones that run commands can also break things. The safer the setting, the slower it feels. That trade is worth it until you trust the workflow.

content.heading: Also worth knowing
content.text: These did not get a full page, but you may meet them at work. Facts come from each vendor's own pages, read on 2 Oct 2026.
table: Code suggestions, inline chat, agentic tasks, and vulnerability scanning in IDEs, a CLI, and the AWS console

Credit-based pricing, with models from several providers.
Open-source (Apache 2.0) agent for VS Code, JetBrains, a CLI, and a desktop app
Asks approval for every edit and command unless you turn on auto-approve. Works with many providers.
Chat, edit, agent mode, and autocomplete in VS Code and JetBrains, plus a CLI
A code editor with an agent panel, edit prediction, and an inline assistant
Bring your own API keys, use local models, or use Zed-hosted ones. Supports external agents.
content.note: Other tools exist too, including JetBrains' own AI features, which I could not confirm from their page.

content.heading: Why a long list does not mean a better choice
bullets: Most of these use the same few underlying models, so the difference is the workflow around them.
Pick two, try both on one small real task, and keep the one that fits.
Ask IT which are approved before you try any of them at work.

content.heading: Why this page exists
content.text: If you use an AI coding assistant for work, your IT or security team decides what is allowed. This checklist helps you ask good questions, so approval takes days, not months.
content.warn: It is your responsibility to get approval before you use a tool on work code or data. These are questions to ask, not answers. This guide is not legal, security, or compliance advice.

content.heading: Questions to bring to IT
table: Is this tool on the approved list? Is a specific plan or account type required?
Must I use a company account, not a personal one? Who pays?
Where is my code sent and stored? For how long? Is it used to train models?
What data classes can I put in a prompt? Which are never allowed (customer data, secrets, regulated data)?
Is single sign-on required? Who can add or remove users?
Are prompts and actions logged? Who can see the logs?
Are plugins, MCP servers, and extensions approved one by one, or blocked?
Which modes are allowed? Is auto or full-auto approval banned?
Does it need to reach the internet? Does it work behind our proxy?
Who owns the output? Are there license or IP rules for AI-written code?
Do we have rules (SOC 2, HIPAA, PCI, export controls) that limit use?
Do I need to say when AI helped write code?

content.heading: Before you ask
bullets: Know which tool, which plan, and which task you want to use it for.
Be ready to say what code or data it would see.
Read the vendor's security and privacy page so your questions are specific.
Write down the answer, with the date and who gave it.

content.heading: What using AI responsibly means
content.text: A coding assistant works like a fast, tireless, eager intern. It will try anything you let it, and it cannot always tell a good idea from a bad one. Using it responsibly means you stay the person in charge of what ships.
bullets: You own the result. If Claude writes it and you ship it, it is your code.
Check the work. Run it, test it, read it. Confident does not mean correct.
Protect other people's data. Customers, coworkers, and patients did not agree to be pasted into a prompt.
Follow your company policy on AI tools, and say so when AI helped build something.
Respect licenses. Do not ship code you cannot trace to a source you are allowed to use.

content.heading: The risks, in plain English
table: Invents a function or setting that does not exist, and says it with total certainty.
A cleanup request removes files you needed. Without git, they may be gone.
Anything you can do on your computer, it can do: install software, move files, change settings.
Passwords and API keys in a file it reads can end up in a prompt, a log, or committed code.
Text in a web page, issue, or file can contain hidden instructions aimed at the AI (prompt injection).
It may install a library that is outdated, unmaintained, or malicious.
If nobody can explain it, nobody can fix it at 2am.

content.heading: Habits that keep you safe
bullets: Start with the most cautious approval setting your tool offers, and read every change and every command.
Use git for everything, and commit before big changes.
Never run it as administrator or in a folder with files you cannot lose.
Never paste passwords, keys, customer data, or health data.
Ask it to explain anything you do not understand, before you accept it.
If something feels off, stop with Escape and ask what it is doing.
content.warn: The risk is not that Claude is careless. It is that it is fast. A mistake you would catch on step two can pile up to step twenty before you look up.

content.heading: Keep secrets out of reach
bullets: Do not keep passwords, keys, or tokens in the project folder. Use a secrets manager or environment variables outside the repo.
Add secret files such as .env to .gitignore so they never reach git.
Many tools can be told to ignore files or deny reading them. Check your tool's docs for how, and turn it on.
If a secret ever reaches a prompt or a commit, treat it as leaked and rotate it.
content.note: Deny rules block in every Claude Code mode, including bypass. Check the permissions docs for the exact rule syntax in your version.

content.heading: Limit the blast radius
bullets: Work on a git branch, and commit before you start.
Use a sandbox, container, or throwaway folder for riskier modes. Claude Code has /sandbox, and Codex sandboxes file access.
Never run an agent as an administrator.
Keep production credentials off any machine where an agent runs unattended.

content.heading: Verify AI-written code
content.text: AI code can look right and be wrong. Treat it like a pull request from someone you have not met.
bullets: Read the diff. If you cannot explain a change, do not merge it.
Run the tests, and add a test for anything new.
Run your linter and a security scanner.
Check any new dependency: does it exist, is it maintained, is it the real package?
Keep changes small, so review stays possible.

content.heading: Watch for prompt injection
content.text: Text in a web page, an issue, a file, or an MCP tool result can contain hidden instructions aimed at the AI. If your assistant reads outside content, it may try to follow them.
content.warn: Be extra careful when an agent can both read untrusted content and take actions like running commands or sending data. Keep approvals on in that situation.

content.heading: How the tools charge
table: A free tier, and paid plans with larger AI credit allowances. Students, teachers, and open source maintainers can qualify for premium features at no cost.
Free with a personal Google login: 60 requests a minute and 1,000 a day. An API key has a free tier of 1,000 requests a day.
Free tier of 50 agentic chat interactions a month; paid options for more.
Credit-based, with different credit costs for different models.
The software is open source. You pay your model provider for what you use.
A Claude subscription or Anthropic Console account. API pricing is per million tokens, with batch requests 50% off.
Sign in with a ChatGPT plan, or use an API key.
Plans and limits change, so read the current pricing page.

content.heading: Habits that save money on any tool
bullets: Use the smallest model that does the job, and move up only when you must.
Plan before you build. A reviewed plan avoids expensive rework.
Start a fresh conversation for each task, because long history costs more on every request.
Be specific. Naming the file and the goal beats "look around and fix it".
Keep instruction files short, since they load every session.
Connect only the extensions and servers you need.
Watch your usage screen or command, and set alerts where the tool offers them.
content.note: Claude-specific commands such as /cost and /clear are covered in the Claude Code deep dive.

content.heading: Requirements
content.text: A terminal, and a Claude subscription or an Anthropic Console account. The recommended installer does not need Node.js. No IDE is required, though VS Code and JetBrains extensions, a desktop app, and a web version exist.

content.heading: Install (recommended)
content.code:
# macOS, Linux, WSL
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash

# Windows PowerShell
irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex

# or Homebrew
brew install --cask claude-code
content.note: Native installs update themselves in the background. Homebrew installs do not, so run brew upgrade now and then.

content.heading: Authenticate
content.code: claude
content.note: You are prompted to log in the first time you run claude. If ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is set, it asks you to approve the key instead.

content.heading: Verify
content.code: claude --version
content.note: If your shell says claude is not found, open a new terminal window. If it still fails, the install folder is not on your PATH yet.

content.heading: First things to do
bullets: 1. Open a terminal in a project you know well (a git repo, not your home folder).
2. Run claude, then ask for an architecture overview to confirm it can read your code.
3. Run /init to generate a starter CLAUDE.md, then edit it with your real conventions.

4. Check which permission mode you are in (Shift+Tab cycles modes). Recent versions can start in auto mode, so run claude --permission-mode default to approve each action until you trust the workflow.
5. Make one small change on a new git branch so it is easy to review or discard.
6. Run /cost to see usage, and /clear between unrelated tasks.
content.note: If you want to learn more, please go to academy.claude.com

content.heading: Courses worth knowing (academy.claude.com)
bullets: AI Fluency: Framework and Foundations: collaborate with AI effectively, ethically, and safely using the 4D framework (about 4 hours)
AI Capabilities and Limitations: build an accurate picture of what language models can and cannot do (about 3.5 hours)
Building Effective Human-Agent Teams (beta): preparing your team for multiplayer AI, best for team leaders (about 45 minutes)
Claude Code 101: the agentic loop, context windows, the Explore, Plan, Code, Commit workflow, CLAUDE.md, subagents, MCP, and hooks (about 1.5 hours; a Claude account or API key is needed)
Claude Code in Action: running longer, less supervised sessions, permission modes, scheduling, GitHub Actions, and verifying unattended work (about 1 hour; assumes you already use Claude Code)
content.note: The Claude Code courses are linked from the Claude Code docs at academy.claude.com/courses/claude-code-101 and academy.claude.com/courses/claude-code-in-action.

content.heading: If you are a creative
bullets: Draft and revise: ask for three different takes on a story, script, or pitch, then merge the best parts.
Build a small personal site or portfolio page and iterate on the design by describing what you want changed.
Put your voice and style rules in CLAUDE.md so drafts sound like you.
Use it as a sounding board: ask it to critique your idea before you commit to it.
content.note: Just like the Green Lanterns, creativity is key. The ring only builds what you can imagine, and Claude works the same way: the clearer and more inventive your idea, the better the result. Specificity begets clarity.

content.heading: If you are a professional
bullets: Ask for an overview of an unfamiliar codebase or document set before you start work.
Automate repetitive chores: tests, release notes, report formatting, data cleanup.
Write team conventions into a project CLAUDE.md and commit it so everyone shares them.
Review every change before merging, and never paste secrets or restricted data (see Safety & Data).

content.heading: Start in a project directory
content.code:
cd your-project
claude
content.note: Claude Code reads your project context on startup — git history, file structure, and any CLAUDE.md files.

content.heading: Useful first prompts
bullets: "What does this codebase do? Give me an architecture overview."
"What are the main entry points?"
"Find all the places where user authentication happens."
"What tests exist and how do I run them?"

content.heading: Three tiers, one idea
content.text: Anthropic ships models in sizes. Small ones are fast and cheap, large ones think harder and cost more. Pick the smallest model that does the job, and move up only when the answer is not good enough.
table: Fastest and cheapest. High-volume, latency-sensitive tasks.
The balance of speed and intelligence. A good everyday default.
Long-running agentic coding and knowledge work.
The top of the lineup, for demanding reasoning and long-horizon agent work.

content.heading: Current models
content.note: Corrected against Anthropic's models overview on 2026-10-07: Haiku 5.5 is the current small model, and Haiku 4.5 is now legacy (see the next table). The docs suggest starting with Opus 5.5 for most workloads and moving to Fable 5.1 when Opus at higher effort still falls short. Batch requests are 50% off.

content.heading: Older models and their status
table: Not sooner than 28 May 2027 / 16 Apr 2027 / 5 Feb 2027
content.note: Status comes from Anthropic's model deprecations page, as read by the original guide on 2 Oct 2026 (not re-checked here). Retired models fail if you call them, and Anthropic gives at least 60 days' notice before retiring a public model. Check that page before you build on any model.

content.heading: Switch models inside Claude Code
content.code: /model
content.note: Look up current prices on the Anthropic pricing page, since they change between generations.

content.heading: What it does
content.text: CLAUDE.md is a markdown file Claude Code reads automatically at the start of every session. It's your standing instructions — conventions, rules, toolchain specifics. Think of it as onboarding documentation for your AI collaborator.

content.heading: Locations
bullets: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md — global, applies to every project
{project}/CLAUDE.md — project-specific rules
{project}/{dir}/CLAUDE.md — subtree rules (applied when working in that folder)

content.heading: Starter template
content.code:
# Project: my-service

## Toolchain
- Package manager: pnpm (never npm or yarn)
- Test runner: vitest — run `pnpm test` before committing
- Linter: biome — `pnpm lint:fix` before pushing

## Architecture
- Hexagonal. Domain layer has zero framework imports.
- New services go in src/domain/services/

## Rules
- Never modify migration files after they've been committed
- No console.log in committed code — use the logger module
- All API endpoints need a corresponding OpenAPI spec entry

content.heading: Which .md file does what
table: When your request matches its description, or when you type /name.
Only if someone opens it. Describes the project to people.
A shared convention across tools. Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md, so point it at AGENTS.md with an @AGENTS.md import.
Not built in. A team convention: a short file explaining why the project exists and what done looks like. Reference it from CLAUDE.md or ask Claude to read it.
Not built in. A saved plan for a task so work survives a /clear.
content.note: The difference in one line: CLAUDE.md is how to work here, intent.md is why we are doing this, a plan is what we do next, and a skill is a recipe.

content.heading: Example intent.md
content.code:
# Intent: invoice-export

## Why
Finance needs a monthly CSV of all invoices. Today it is done by hand.

## Done means
- One command produces the CSV
- Totals match the billing dashboard
- No customer emails appear in the file

## Not in scope
- PDF export
- Changing the invoice database schema

content.heading: What NOT to put in CLAUDE.md
bullets: Secrets, API keys, or credentials
Long explanations — keep it terse and actionable
Things Claude already knows (standard patterns, common libraries)
Everything — longer is not better. Be surgical.

content.heading: What skills are
content.text: Skills are folders containing a SKILL.md file that defines a reusable workflow. Type /skill-name to run one, or let Claude pick it up on its own when your request matches its description. Great for repetitive multi-step tasks.

content.heading: Create a skill
content.code:
# Skills live in:
~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md   # global
.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md      # project-only

# Create one:
mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills/standup
vim ~/.claude/skills/standup/SKILL.md

content.heading: Example: /standup skill
content.code:
---
name: standup
description: Generate a daily standup from git history. Use when the user asks for a standup, daily update, or what they did yesterday.
---

# Daily Standup

1. Run `git log --oneline --since="yesterday midnight" --until="midnight" --author="$(git config user.name)"`
2. Run `git status` to see in-progress work
3. Output format:

**Yesterday:** [bullets from commits]
**Today:** [in-progress items]
**Blockers:** [any / none]

content.heading: What triggers a skill automatically
content.text: Every skill has a short description at the top of its SKILL.md. Claude reads the descriptions, and when your request matches one, it loads that skill without you typing anything. So the description is the trigger.
bullets: Your words: asking to "review this PR" can load a review skill.
The task: writing tests, planning, debugging, or deploying can load the skill built for it.
The files: working in a certain language or framework can match a skill written for it.
You: typing /skill-name always runs it, no matching needed.
content.note: Write descriptions as "Use when ..." with the exact situations you want. Vague descriptions fire at the wrong times or never.

content.heading: Skill vs. plugin
content.text: A skill is one recipe. A plugin is a package that can bundle several skills, slash commands, subagents, hooks, and MCP servers so a whole team installs the same setup in one step.
content.code: /plugin
content.note: Run /plugin to browse and install plugins. Treat plugins like any software you install: only use ones from sources you trust, because they can run code on your machine.

content.heading: Useful skills to build
bullets: /standup — generate daily standup from git log
/review — run a structured code review on a file
/deploy-check — verify the project is ready to deploy
/doc — generate documentation for a function or module
/test — write tests for a specific file or function

content.heading: What an MCP server is
content.text: MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard for plugging outside tools into Claude. An MCP server gives Claude new abilities: read your GitHub issues, query a database, check a calendar, drive a browser. Without one, Claude only sees your files and terminal.

content.heading: Add and inspect servers
content.code:
claude mcp add <name> -- <command>   # add a server
claude mcp list                      # see what is connected
/mcp                                 # status inside a session

content.heading: MCP vs. skills vs. plugins
table: Connects Claude to an outside system
Read and comment on GitHub issues
How we do a code review here
A bundle of skills, commands, hooks, and servers

content.heading: Rules of thumb
bullets: Connect only the servers a task needs. Each one adds tool descriptions to the context, which costs money and can distract Claude.
Prefer read-only access. A server that can only read cannot delete anything.
Use a limited account or token for each server, never your admin credentials.
content.warn: An MCP server acts with your accounts and permissions. A server that can send email, write to a database, or push code can do that wrong just as fast as it can do it right.

content.heading: You choose how much to trust it
content.text: Claude Code can read files, edit files, and run commands. The permission mode decides how often it has to stop and ask you. Press Shift+Tab to cycle between modes. Recent versions (v2.1.283 and later) start new terminal and VS Code sessions in auto mode, so check which mode you are in before you begin.
table: Reads only. Asks before edits, commands, and network access.
Reads, file edits, and common file commands like mkdir, mv, cp
Reads only. No edits until you approve a plan.
Everything, while a second model reviews each action in the background
Only tools you pre-approved. Everything else is denied.
Low. Meant for CI and scripts.

content.heading: Start in Manual mode
content.note: Manual is the mode that reviews every action. Its config value is "default".

content.heading: Make a plan first
content.text: Planning costs a little and saves a lot. A plan lets you catch a wrong approach before any file changes, instead of after twenty.
bullets: 1. Press Shift+Tab until you reach plan mode.
2. Describe the goal, the limits, and what done looks like.
3. Let Claude explore and write the plan. It cannot change anything yet.
4. Read it. Ask for changes. Ask what could go wrong.
5. Approve it, then work in Manual or Accept edits mode.
6. Save the plan to PLAN.md so it survives /clear.

content.heading: Plan template
content.code:
# Plan: add CSV export

## Goal
One command exports last month's invoices to CSV.

## Constraints
- No schema changes
- Do not touch the billing module

## Steps
1. Add export function in src/export/invoices.ts
2. Add a test with 3 sample invoices
3. Wire up the CLI command

## Verify
- npm test passes
- Output totals match the dashboard

content.heading: Manually accepting edits
content.text: In Manual mode, Claude shows each change as a diff: red lines are removed, green lines are added. You press accept or reject. Reading the diff is the whole point, so do not hold the accept key down without looking.
content.warn: The risk of skipping review: a small mistake lands in your project and you do not find out until it breaks something real. If you cannot explain what a change does, reject it and ask Claude to explain.

content.heading: Auto mode: what you are agreeing to
content.text: Auto mode saves you from clicking approve a hundred times. A second model reviews each action in the background and blocks the risky ones, but that is a safety check, not a guarantee. You are still trusting Claude to make many small decisions without you.
bullets: It can edit or delete many files in one go.
It can run commands that install software or change your system.
A wrong guess early on can snowball into many wrong steps before you look.
content.warn: If you are new to coding, set Manual mode as your default. Use auto mode only on a git branch with everything saved, in a folder that holds nothing you cannot afford to lose, and only for tasks you could review afterward.

content.heading: Safety net before you give Claude more freedom
bullets: Work on a git branch, and commit before you start.
Keep secrets out of the project folder, or in a file Claude is told to ignore.
Know the undo: git diff shows what changed, git restore puts files back.
Run the tests after every task, not only at the end.

content.heading: What Claude Code can see
bullets: Files you are working in (reads them when needed)
Git history and status
Terminal output from commands it runs
Environment variables (be careful with secrets)

content.heading: What Claude Code cannot do
bullets: Access files outside your project without explicit permission
Make network calls directly (only via tools you approve)
Run commands without showing them to you first (in Manual mode)

content.heading: Data classification rules
bullets: Never paste production data (PII, credentials, PHI) into Claude Code prompts
Treat Claude Code conversations as internal-confidential by default
If you're unsure whether data is safe to share, don't share it
Use sanitized/synthetic data for examples in prompts

content.heading: Review before accepting
content.text: Claude Code shows you every file it wants to modify. Read the diff before accepting. You are responsible for code you ship. In Manual mode Claude asks first. In auto mode it acts on its own, so you review the results afterward.

content.heading: How billing works
content.text: Claude Code needs a Claude subscription or an Anthropic Console account. With API billing you pay per token (input and output). Either way, cost depends on the model you pick and how much context each request carries, so a quick question is cheap and a long, sprawling session is not. Run /cost to see where you stand.

content.heading: Cost control tips
bullets: Use the smallest model that works. Haiku or Sonnet for routine work, Opus only when you are stuck (switch with /model).
Plan first. A reviewed plan avoids expensive rework and wrong turns.
Use /clear between unrelated tasks, and /compact to shrink a long session.
Be specific. Naming the file and the goal beats "look around and fix it".
Keep CLAUDE.md short, since it loads every session.
Connect only the MCP servers you need. Each one adds to every request.
Install the cost tracker Stop hook to see per-turn cost in real time
Set COST_ALERT_12H and COST_ALERT_DAY env vars to get spend alerts

content.heading: Install the cost tracker
content.code:
git clone https://github.com/thejaredchapman/claude-code-usage-guard
cd claude-code-usage-guard
bash install.sh

content.heading: What it is
content.text: Anthropic's agentic coding tool. It reads your codebase, edits files, runs commands, and connects to your dev tools. It runs in the terminal, VS Code, JetBrains, a desktop app, and the web, and all of them share the same engine, CLAUDE.md files, settings, and MCP servers.

content.heading: Get started
content.code:
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash   # macOS, Linux, WSL
cd your-project
claude

content.heading: How to use it
bullets: Run claude in a project and log in when prompted.
Press Shift+Tab to see and change the permission mode.
Use plan mode for anything bigger than a small edit.
Put rules in CLAUDE.md, recipes in skills, and automatic actions in hooks.
Use /clear between tasks and /cost to watch spend.

content.heading: Pros and cons
pros: Works across files and tools, including git, commits, and pull requests.
Extensible: CLAUDE.md, skills, hooks, subagents, MCP servers, and an Agent SDK.
Several permission modes let you set how closely it is watched.
Same setup in terminal, IDEs, desktop, and web.
Can also read an AGENTS.md written for other tools.
cons: Anthropic models by default; other providers only through some setups.
Most surfaces need a Claude subscription or Anthropic Console account.
Costs can grow on long sessions with lots of context.
Terminal-first, which is a learning curve for beginners.

content.heading: Keep it safe
content.warn: Recent versions can start in auto mode. Switch to Manual with claude --permission-mode default until you have a git branch and tests to catch mistakes.

content.heading: What it is
content.text: GitHub's assistant. Per GitHub's docs it responds while you work (suggesting code, answering questions, explaining code), handles multi-step agent tasks (researching a repo, proposing plans, editing files, preparing pull requests), and can be customized with instructions, prompts, and custom agents. It also works with MCP servers and third-party coding agents.

content.heading: Get started
content.code:
# 1. Try Copilot Free or subscribe to a paid plan.
# 2. Through an organization? Request access at
#    github.com/settings/copilot
# 3. Install the extension in your editor and sign in.
#
# Documented editors: VS Code, Visual Studio, JetBrains IDEs,
# Xcode, Eclipse, Vim/Neovim, Azure Data Studio.

content.heading: How to use it
bullets: Accept suggestions as you type, and read each one first.
Ask chat to explain code, plan a task, or refactor.
Use agent features for multi-step work and review the pull request it prepares.
Add custom instructions so it follows your conventions.

content.heading: Pros and cons
pros: A free tier exists, so you can try it at no cost.
Students, teachers, and open source maintainers can qualify for premium features at no cost.
Works in many editors, from VS Code and JetBrains to Xcode and Neovim.
Built into GitHub, so it fits pull requests and code review.
Business and Enterprise plans for organizations.
cons: What you get depends on your plan, including its AI credit allowance.
Models and features vary by plan, so check what yours includes.
Suggestions can look right and still be wrong.
Less of a standalone, scriptable terminal workflow than the CLI agents.

content.heading: Keep it safe
content.warn: Suggestions are easy to accept by reflex. Read them as carefully as code from a stranger, especially around security and data handling.

content.heading: What it is
content.text: An AI code editor that Cursor describes as "a coding agent for building ambitious software". It offers Tab and inline editing, chat, an agent mode for complex tasks, codebase understanding, and code review. It supports 50+ models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and others.

content.heading: Get started
content.code:
# Download Cursor from cursor.com
# macOS 12+ (.dmg), Windows 10+ (.exe),
# Linux (apt, dnf, or AppImage)
# Open the app, finish setup, and open your project folder.

content.heading: How to use it
bullets: Use Tab and inline editing for quick changes as you type.
Use chat to ask about the project.
Use agent mode for bigger tasks, and review the diff.
Customize it with rules, skills, MCP servers, and plugins.

content.heading: Pros and cons
pros: Choose from 50+ models across several providers.
Tab, chat, and agent are all inside one editor.
Customizable with plugins, skills, MCP, and rules.
Connects to GitHub, GitLab, Azure DevOps, Bitbucket, Slack, Linear, and more.
cons: You work inside its editor, so you have to switch.
Plans and usage limits change, so read the current pricing page.
Your code goes to cloud models, so check company policy first.
Agent edits can be large and easy to over-accept.

content.heading: Keep it safe
content.warn: Cursor makes accepting changes very smooth. Slow down on agent edits and read the diff for every file before you accept.

content.heading: What it is
content.text: Windsurf is now called Devin Desktop, an AI IDE with an agent called Cascade. Cognition, the maker of Devin, acquired Windsurf in July 2025 and announced the rename in June 2026, according to press reports. The docs describe it as a standalone IDE, not VS Code-based, and some URLs and package names still say "windsurf".

content.heading: Get started
content.code:
# Download for Mac, Windows, or Linux from the Windsurf / Devin Desktop site.
# Setup: pick a theme, optionally import VS Code or Cursor settings,
# sign in, then start your first AI session.

content.heading: How to use it
bullets: Describe a task to the agent in plain language.
Watch which files it touches and review each change.
Add memories and rules so it follows your conventions.
Use workflows for repeated tasks and MCP servers for outside tools.

content.heading: Pros and cons
pros: Memories and rules customize how it behaves.
Workflows automate repetitive tasks.
One-click app deploys.
Can import your VS Code or Cursor settings.
cons: The product was renamed in 2026, so names in docs and packages can differ.
It is a standalone IDE, so you have to adopt it.
Some extensions are incompatible, including other AI completion tools.
Agent actions still need careful review.

content.heading: Keep it safe
content.warn: When an agent can run terminal commands, read each command before approving it. Never approve a command you do not understand.

content.heading: What it is
content.text: OpenAI's coding agent. It comes as a terminal CLI, an IDE integration (VS Code, Cursor, Windsurf), a desktop app, and Codex Web, a cloud agent at chatgpt.com/codex. The CLI is open source under the Apache-2.0 license.

content.heading: Get started
content.code:
# macOS / Linux
curl -fsSL https://chatgpt.com/codex/install.sh | sh
# or: npm install -g @openai/codex
# or: brew install --cask codex

cd your-project
codex

content.heading: How to use it
bullets: Sign in with ChatGPT, or use an API key.
Describe a task, for example "Tell me about this project".
Pick permissions: Review mode asks before acting, Autonomous mode does not. Adjust per session with /permissions.
Run /init to create an AGENTS.md of project instructions.

content.heading: Pros and cons
pros: Open-source CLI under Apache-2.0.
Choice of terminal, IDE, desktop app, or cloud.
Works with a ChatGPT plan sign-in.
Sandboxing limits file access and writable folders.
AGENTS.md is a convention several tools share.
cons: OpenAI models only.
Cloud tasks run in a sandbox with limits on what they can reach.
Plan and sign-in options affect what you can use.
Results still need a human review before you merge.

content.heading: Keep it safe
content.warn: Autonomous mode edits files and runs commands without asking. Use it only in a disposable folder or container, never on your main machine with real credentials.

content.heading: What it is
content.text: Google's open-source (Apache 2.0) terminal agent. It has built-in file operations, shell commands, web fetching, and Google Search grounding, and it supports MCP servers.

content.heading: Get started
content.code:
npm install -g @google/gemini-cli
# or run without installing: npx @google/gemini-cli
# also available through Homebrew, MacPorts, and Anaconda

cd your-project
gemini

content.heading: How to use it
bullets: Sign in with a Google account when prompted.
Describe a task or ask about the codebase.
Use gemini -p "question" for a one-off, non-interactive prompt.
Choose a model with -m, and add project guidance in GEMINI.md.

content.heading: Pros and cons
pros: Open source under Apache 2.0.
Free tier with a personal Google login: 60 requests a minute and 1,000 a day.
1M token context window with Gemini 3 models.
Web fetch, Google Search grounding, and MCP support built in.
cons: Gemini models only.
Free-tier request limits can interrupt long sessions.
Quality varies by task, so test it on your own work.
Fewer ready-made workflows than the most mature agents.

content.heading: Keep it safe
content.warn: The free tier is a good reason to try it, not a reason to relax. It can edit files and run commands, so read each action it asks to take.

content.heading: What it is
content.text: An open-source terminal pair programmer. You choose which files it can see, tell it what to change, and it edits them. By default it commits every change to git with a descriptive message, so each step is easy to undo.

content.heading: Get started
content.code:
python -m pip install aider-install   # Python 3.8-3.13
aider-install

cd your-project
aider --model sonnet --api-key anthropic=<key>
# other examples: --model o3-mini --api-key openai=<key>

content.heading: How to use it
bullets: Add files with /add so it can edit them.
Ask questions without editing anything with /ask.
Request changes with /code.
Use /architect for a two-model plan-and-edit flow.
Undo an aider commit with /undo.

content.heading: Pros and cons
pros: Works with many model providers, so you pick the model.
Every edit is a git commit, so rollback is simple.
Open source; you pay only for the API you use.
Lightweight and runs in any terminal.
cons: Terminal only, with a plain interface.
You bring your own API key and manage which files are in context.
Needs a supported Python version.
Less hands-off than agents that plan and run everything themselves.

content.heading: Keep it safe
content.warn: Because it commits each change, you get a built-in safety net. Still read each diff, and keep your API key out of any file you commit.
